name: Diaphragmatic breathing

lead: Diaphragmatic breathing, also called belly breathing, uses the diaphragm for slow, deep breaths. In voice work it is used to get steadier, fuller delivery and more presence when you speak.

The diaphragm descends on inhalation, expanding the abdomen, and controlled exhalation underpins steady phonation, which voice teachers link to a stronger, more resonant sound. Published research examines it mainly for relaxation, stress and respiratory conditions; none tests it for changing pitch or voice appearance.

paras: People inhale slowly through the nose so the belly rises, then exhale slowly, often through pursed lips, and carry that breath control into speaking or reading aloud. It is practised in short daily sessions and is commonly paired with other voice exercises.
No serious adverse effects are described. Overdoing deep breathing can cause light-headedness for some people.

angle.text: Belly breathing is practised to support the voice so it sounds steadier, fuller and more present. Deeper breath support allows smoother, controlled phonation. It is studied for stress and respiratory care, and its effect on how a voice sounds is untested.

lead: Diaphragmatic breathing, also called belly or abdominal breathing, is a technique that uses the diaphragm to take deep breaths, typically by inhaling slowly through the nose and exhaling through pursed lips.[1][2] It is used in respiratory care, in stress and anxiety management, and in voice training, where it is associated with breath support.[1][2][3]

In looksmaxxing discussion of the voice, it is mentioned as a way to improve breath control and to deepen vocal tone. Grokipedia states that it is integrated into voice training for men to address insufficient breath support and to deepen tone through chest resonance and breath control.[2] Acoustics references, by contrast, report that the chest contributes little to vocal resonance,[4] and no studies were found testing diaphragmatic breathing for changing voice pitch or appearance.
Published research examines it mainly for relaxation, stress and respiratory conditions.
infobox: Belly breathing, abdominal breathing, deep breathing
Stress, respiratory conditions, voice and singing support
Studied for stress and respiratory use; none for appearance

paras: The diaphragm is a dome-shaped muscle separating the chest and abdominal cavities; it descends on inhalation and relaxes on exhalation, and is the main muscle of quiet inspiration.[2] The technique emphasises abdominal expansion rather than chest elevation, and can be done lying, sitting or standing.[1][2]

Singing pedagogy describes breath for singing in four stages: inhalation, setting up controls, controlled exhalation and recovery. Teachers say these should be consciously controlled until automatic, and that posture and abdominal or chest tension can restrict airflow.[5]

Speech-language pathology uses diaphragmatic breathing as part of the Accent Method, which pairs it with rhythmic vowel play.[6] Such uses concern voice function and disorders rather than lowering pitch.

In a randomised study of 40 healthy adults reported in 2017, a diaphragmatic breathing group was compared with a control group on attention, negative affect and cortisol responses to stress.[7] A 2019 JBI systematic review examined the effectiveness of diaphragmatic breathing for reducing physiological and psychological stress in adults.[8] Reviews of breathing techniques in serious respiratory illness are reported to support relief of shortness of breath, with mixed results for exercise tolerance in COPD.[1] No studies were found on diaphragmatic breathing for voice pitch or appearance.
